focus: Deep-learning convolution is cross-correlation with no kernel flip. A learned kernel absorbs the flip, so the distinction changes nothing in a trained layer.
Output size per axis is \(\left\lfloor (n + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s + 1 \right\rfloor\). With odd \(k\) and matching same padding each output centers on its input pixel.
Groups split channels into \(G\) independent convolutions. Parameters and multiply-adds fall by \(G\), while output shape is unchanged. Groups equal to \(C_{\text{in}}\) is depthwise convolution.
A \(1 \times 1\) convolution is a per-pixel linear map across channels. Stacked \(1 \times 1\) layers need a nonlinearity between them or they fold into one linear map.

Use same-shape padding to reason about equivariance and residual adds.

traps: Counting padding once in the formula. D2L and PyTorch \(p\) means padding on both sides, so the total added rows are \(2p\).

fit.note: D2L pooling and transposed-conv pages with UDL receptive-field sections cover both topics at derive depth, and UDL problems give checked practice.

focus: Receptive field grows by \((k-1)\) times the product of earlier strides per layer. Stride-2 downsampling doubles the growth rate while quartering activations.

One conv layer holds \(C_{\text{out}}\) times \((C_{\text{in}}/G)\) times \(kH\) times \(kW\) weights plus \(C_{\text{out}}\) biases, and costs about twice that many FLOPs per output position for the multiply-add.
Pooling has no parameters, acts per channel, and \(2 \times 2\) stride-2 pooling quarters resolution. Max-pooling gives limited shift tolerance inside a window, not invariance.
A transposed convolution applies the transpose of a downsampling weight matrix. It learns an upsampling and is not an inverse of any forward convolution.

next.note: Test which of these mechanisms preserve or break translation equivariance.
Compare receptive-field growth with patch tokenization of images.

outcomes: Derive receptive-field growth across stride, kernel and dilation choices.

selfTest.a: Networks usually double the channels after downsampling. Convolution cost scales with positions times \(C_{\text{in}}\) times \(C_{\text{out}}\), so doubling both channel counts restores the FLOPs exactly, while activation memory only halves.
No. It applies the transposed weight matrix with its own learned weights, so equal shape back does not mean equal values.
selfTest.q: Does a transposed convolution invert the convolution with the same weights?
\(2 \times 2\) stride-2 max-pooling. Which input shifts leave the output unchanged?
selfTest.a: A shift by 2 pixels shifts the output by one cell (equivariance on the coarse grid). A one-pixel shift leaves an output unchanged only when that window's maximum stays inside the window, which depends on the data; test with a shifted copy.

focus: Convolution is equivariant to translation in the interior. Stride, pooling and zero-padded borders break exact equivariance, and pooling trades it for local tolerance.
Zero padding leaks absolute position. The network can learn where the whitespace border is.
A residual block fits the difference from identity, so pushing branch weights toward zero recovers a shallower net. The unraveled sum gives \(2^K\) paths for \(K\) blocks.
Each residual addition grows activation variance under standard initialization. Per-channel batch normalization, or branch rescaling, keeps the forward stable.

focus: \(H_t = \phi(X_t W_{xh} + H_{t-1} W_{hh} + b_h)\) reuses the same three matrices every step. Sequence length adds depth, not parameters.
BPTT sums per-step losses whose gradients chain products of hidden Jacobians. Regular truncation at \(\tau\) drops all paths longer than \(\tau\) and biases long-dependency learning.
Clip by global norm \(g \gets \min(1, \theta/\|g\|) g\) after unrolling. It bounds the step, not the Jacobian product, so it treats explosion, not vanishing.
Detaching the hidden state between batches stops gradients but keeps the values. Truncated BPTT still learns only within-segment dependencies.

units.title: Recurrent cells, unrolling and backpropagation through time
traps: Averaging the loss over time and thinking truncation is then unbiased. Truncation drops long paths whatever the reduction.
Carrying hidden state across batches and calling it full BPTT. Values carry but gradients do not unless the graph does.
Clipping to fix non-learning from vanishing. Clipping only caps large steps, so vanishing needs architecture or objective changes.
units.why: Unrolling turns a loop into a deep shared-weight network. BPTT is backprop on that unrolled graph, and truncation decides which dependencies the gradient can ever see.

fit.note: D2L BPTT detail with GRU and LSTM scratch pages covers both topics, and the numbered end-of-page exercises give named practice without new material.

focus: \(dL/dh_t\) fans out through powers of \(W_{hh}\) transposed. Eigenvalues below 1 decay geometrically and above 1 grow geometrically, and tanh or sigmoid derivatives shrink most steps further.

GRU: \(R\) gates how much past state enters the candidate, and \(Z\) interpolates old state with candidate. LSTM splits the same job across \(F\) for erase, \(I\) for write and \(O\) for reveal, with a separate cell \(C_t\).
With \(F=1\) and \(I=0\) the cell holds its value exactly and gradients flow unchanged. That constant-error path is the whole point.

PyTorch and D2L agree on the update gate: \(z\) weights the old state. They differ on the reset gate: D2L multiplies \(R\) into the state before \(W_{hh}\), while `torch.nn.GRU` applies \(r\) after the recurrent matmul and its bias, \(r \cdot (W_{hn} h + b_{hn})\). Implement the PyTorch form when you match `torch.nn.GRU`.

units.title: Hidden state, encoder-decoder models and teacher forcing
traps: Evaluating statefully after training statelessly, or the reverse. Hidden-state lifetime is part of the model contract, so changing it silently shifts results.
Reading low teacher-forced loss as generation quality. The loss never scores the model's own continuations, so greedy rollout and BLEU do that in the next unit.
Padding the decoder input and forgetting the label shift. Decoder input drops the final token and labels drop `<bos>`, so misaligning by one trains every position on the wrong target.
units.why: State lifetime and teacher forcing are silent evaluation bugs. A model that trains on truth and tests on its own guesses fails exactly where the demo looked best.

fit.note: Practice failed for packed sequences: neither the D2L route nor UDL covers them, so the PyTorch packing reference fills recognition-depth coverage beside CS231n captioning and the D2L beam exercise.

focus: Greedy decoding feeds each `argmax` back with `<bos>` start and `<eos>` stop. Beam search keeps \(k\) hypotheses with length normalization, so larger \(k\) costs linearly more for usually better sequences.
Masked loss divides by valid tokens, not by batch times steps. Dividing by the padded size silently down-weights short-sequence batches.
Packing skips pad steps in the RNN so pads cost nothing and contribute no state. It needs `lengths` and, by default, length-sorted batches.

A leak test perturbs what should not matter, such as pad values, future tokens or carried state, and asserts that valid outputs do not change: bit-identical for a causal RNN on CPU, and within a tight tolerance wherever a kernel may reorder sums.

next.note: Padding and causal masks generalize these loss masks.

selfTest.a: 7: \(5 + 2\) valid tokens. Summing over 10 positions would dilute the short sequence.
selfTest.q: Batch of lengths 5 and 2 padded to 5. What is the masked-loss denominator?
In D2L's greedy-search example, greedy scores 0.048 while picking a different second token gives 0.054. Why does greedy miss it, and what does beam search change?
selfTest.a: Greedy takes the most likely token at each step and never revisits. The other second token is less likely by itself but makes the later tokens more likely. Beam search keeps \(k\) partial sequences, so it can keep that branch alive long enough to see the payoff, though it is not guaranteed to find the best sequence.

selfTest.q: The D2L beam score divides the log-probability by \(L^{\alpha}\), with \(\alpha\) 0.75. What does raising \(\alpha\) do?
selfTest.a: It favors longer outputs. Log-probabilities are negative and grow in magnitude with length, so a larger divisor for long sequences offsets more of that penalty. \(\alpha\) 0 recovers the raw log-probability, which favors short outputs.
Yes. Valid outputs must not depend on pad contents, so the change shows padding leaking into the representation or the loss.

units.title: Decoding, variable-length batches and leak tests
traps: Averaging masked loss over all positions including pads. Short sequences then count less per token, so always divide by the mask sum.
Sorting by length for packing and forgetting to unsort for metrics. Either restore the original order yourself or pass `enforce_sorted=False` and let PyTorch track the permutation.
Stopping generation at fixed `num_steps` instead of `<eos>`. Tail pads then enter BLEU and length statistics as fake content.
units.why: Decoding and masking turn a trained seq2seq net into honest predictions. One unmasked pad token or one peeking future input invalidates every number above it.
